title: Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector
gist: Dataiku's 575 Lab open-sourced Kiji Inspector, which trains sparse autoencoders on the activations of an agent's tool-selection decision token in open-weight models (Gemma 4, Nemotron 3) to explain why a tool was chosen, with causal ablation evidence; Hapke positions it as a causal alternative to chain-of-thought for audit, debugging and drift monitoring, usable only with self-hosted open models.

insights.claim: Hannes Hapke argues that prompt engineering, behavioral testing and chain of thought do not provide causality for agent decisions, only plausible narratives about root causes.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Existing agent observability (traces, CoT) is insufficient for audit; opens a market for interpretability tooling.
insights.locator: The Problem: Opaque Agent Decisions

insights.claim: Kiji Inspector's explanations are derived directly from the activation at a given layer when the decision token is generated, unlike chain of thought, which can state two intended actions and then execute fifteen others with no connection.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Activation-based explanations offer a stronger audit trail than model self-reports.
insights.locator: Then you can take those themes

insights.claim: Traces show which tool an agent selected but cannot explain why; Kiji Inspector generates an additional log explaining the selection, which Hapke pitches for audit and compliance.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Regulated enterprises deploying agents need 'why' logs — a compliance tooling opportunity.

themes.theme: SAE method on the decision token

insights.claim: Sparse autoencoders widen model activations into a larger feature space while forcing roughly 95% of features to zero, separating polysemantic neurons into interpretable features.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Core mechanism behind the mechanistic interpretability tooling wave.
insights.locator: The cool thing about this concept

insights.claim: Unlike prior OpenAI and Eleuther sparse autoencoder work covering entire LLM generations, Kiji Inspector focuses on the agent's decision token rather than averaging activations across the whole prompt.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Narrowing interpretability to decisions makes it tractable for production agents.
insights.locator: What we have tried to do

insights.claim: Kiji Inspector is trained on 1 million synthetic samples forming 500,000 contrastive pairs, each pairing a correct 'anchor' tool choice with a similar-looking adversarial request needing a different tool (e.g., 'how do I reset my password?' vs. 'I tried to reset my password three times').
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Contrastive data design isolates the features that drive tool selection.
insights.locator: Then, how do we actually focus

insights.claim: The decision token is isolated by forcing the agent to respond 'I will use [blank]', with the available tools listed in the prompt, so the next token is the tool name.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Simple, replicable trick for instrumenting tool choice.
insights.locator: Then, how do we actually focus

insights.claim: Kiji Inspector uses a JumpReLU activation whose threshold is learned during training to decide which features are relevant.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Technical detail relevant to SAE quality.

insights.claim: Layer choice is more art than science: early layers have not conceptualized the prompt, while late layers — especially in MoE models like Nemotron 3 with varying routing — yield high error and concepts too abstract for humans, so Hapke's team chose layer 20.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Interpretability quality depends on non-trivial tuning, raising adoption cost.

insights.claim: In Kiji Inspector's Nemotron 3 layer-20 SAE, about 2,688 input dimensions were widened to 10,000; just over 80% of features were alive, under 0.2% completely dead, and 668 features were highly relevant to the investigated tool selections.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Shows a compact feature set governs tool choice, enabling targeted monitoring.

insights.claim: A linear probe on raw activations reached almost 80% accuracy at predicting correct versus incorrect tool selection, while clustering raw activations performed worse than a coin flip, which Hapke cites as justification for the sparse autoencoder step.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Raw activations are not directly interpretable; SAE tooling adds real signal.
insights.quote: You're better off flipping a coin than actually clustering.

insights.claim: Zeroing out the top 10 SAE-relevant activations changed tool selection for 23 contrast types with low p-values, better than random flipping, though some tools could not be shown causal; Hapke notes he is not a statistician.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Early causal evidence supports activation-level steering and auditing, with methodological caveats.
insights.locator: The way this works is for our experiment

insights.claim: Kiji Inspector incorporates Eleuther's token-level fuzzing, swapping individual tokens to test how activations and outcomes change, plus causal validation to distinguish causation from correlation.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Built-in validation improves credibility of explanations.
insights.locator: I think that was for us the interesting

insights.claim: Kiji Inspector is fully open source, shipped as a PyPI package with Docker containers and trained SAEs on Hugging Face for Gemma 4 and Nemotron 3, positioned as model-agnostic versus Google's model-specific Gemma Scope, which lacks a training pipeline.
insights.speaker: Hannes Hapke
insights.so_what: Dataiku uses open responsible-AI tooling for positioning in enterprise AI governance.

insights.claim: Dataiku provides a vLLM patch to return layer activations alongside responses because vLLM and SGLang do not expose them, and hopes to upstream it so hosting platforms like Baseten can offer the feature.

insights.claim: Hapke lists Kiji Inspector use cases as detecting agent misbehavior such as wrong tool picks, audit compliance, validating prompt engineering via activations, and monitoring production drift by watching activation changes over time.

insights.claim: Planned Kiji Inspector work includes supporting more open models such as Qwen, multi-layer experiments combining early and late layers, and testing whether SAE features transfer across models.

insights.so_what: Cross-model transfer, if it works, would lower interpretability costs materially.
